units.text: Start at the local Kubernetes panel. EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes on your infrastructure. Local placement gives you control, but also makes cluster operations part of your responsibility.
Move to the operations panel. You manage the control plane, worker nodes, networking and storage. Plan upgrades and backups as operating work, with recovery procedures you can test.

Inspect the dependency checklist. Registries, identity, DNS and package access must work in the intended environment. For disconnected operation, prepare the required artifacts and local services before losing connectivity.

With the full slide visible, compare the right-hand example. EKS Hybrid Nodes use an AWS-hosted control plane. EKS Anywhere uses a customer-operated local control plane; choose according to connectivity needs and operational ownership.

Begin with registration on the left. Supported external servers or virtual machines join through Systems Manager and the ECS agent. Verify the host's requirements and permissions before scheduling work.

Move to the orchestration panel. ECS manages supported tasks on external capacity, while you provision and maintain the hosts. AWS orchestration does not transfer ownership of the underlying machines.

Inspect the network and storage panel. Design inbound access, host networking, storage and load balancing explicitly. Verify which integrations are supported rather than assuming the same behavior as an AWS-hosted deployment.

Return to the full slide and the disconnected example. Running tasks can continue when AWS connectivity is lost, but cloud scheduling and management cannot communicate changes. Application dependencies can still interrupt useful service.

Start with the dependency inventory in the upper left. Record identity, DNS, secrets, registries, databases and external APIs. A local process may still depend on a remote service for every useful request.

Move to the upper-right categories. Identify what continues locally, what degrades and what requires regional connectivity. Evaluate individual operations, including startup and credential refresh, rather than labeling the whole application offline-capable.

Inspect the lower-left replication panel. Cache or replicate only when consistency, security and staleness requirements allow it. Define how much divergence is acceptable and how updates will be reconciled.

With the full slide restored, follow the recovery sequence. Test disconnection and reconnection, credential expiry and reconciliation. Prove that the system recovers safely, not just that existing processes remain running.
Begin with the requirement in the upper left. This case needs local low-latency processing, resilient AWS connectivity and encryption for sensitive traffic. Keep these as separate design obligations.

Move to the upper-right choices. Select local compute according to operational ownership and service dependencies. Use diverse network paths, checking whether seemingly independent connections share a failure domain.

Inspect the lower-left controls. Specify encryption endpoints, routing preferences, backup capacity and access controls. State exactly which traffic is protected and how the backup path carries the critical workload.

Return to the complete checklist. Test device, circuit and regional-dependency failures, then measure application recovery. Document the operational and cost tradeoffs that explain why the design meets the original requirements.
